chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Building Blocks of a DCF

lessons.title: Forecasting Revenue, Margins and Reinvestment Without Fooling Yourself

children.text: You now know how to turn a forecast into free cash flow and how to discount it. But a DCF is only as good as the forecast feeding it, and this is where most valuations quietly go wrong. Not through bad arithmetic, but through assumptions that are individually plausible and collectively impossible: 20% growth with no extra investment, margins that expand every year in a competitive industry, or a "conservative" base case that beats anything the company has ever achieved. This lesson shows you how to build a forecast that holds together, and how to catch yourself when it does not.

body.text: A forecast is not three separate guesses about revenue, margins and investment. It is one story, and the numbers must agree with each other. Most DCF errors are not math errors. They are story errors.

children.text: The Forecasting Chain
Every FCFF forecast follows the same chain. Each link depends on the one before it.

body.caption: From revenue to free cash flow

cells: Volume × price, or market size × share
Cost structure, pricing power, cycle position
Capex net of depreciation, plus working capital
The return on new capital this implies

children.text: Link 1: Revenue
Break revenue into its real drivers wherever you can. A single growth percentage hides everything that matters.

body.caption: Revenue drivers for common Indian businesses

cells: Quarterly presentations, capacity announcements, industry demand data
Stores × revenue per store, split into same-store growth and new stores
Units sold × average realisation per unit
Monthly sales data released by manufacturers
Headcount × revenue per employee, or deal wins and client growth
Loan book × net interest margin, plus fee income

children.text: Then check your growth rates against
base rates

. Across large samples of listed companies globally, sustaining very high revenue growth for a decade is rare, and growth rates tend to fade toward the growth of the wider economy as companies get bigger. India's nominal GDP has grown at roughly 10% to 12% a year over long periods, which is a useful anchor for where a large company's growth eventually settles.

markDefs.definition: How often something has happened across a large group of comparable cases. For forecasting, how frequently companies of similar size have actually sustained a given growth rate.

body.title: Revenue index (year 0 = 100): 25% forever vs growth that fades to 9%

children.text: After ten years, the constant 25% forecast shows revenue at 931 against 390 for the fading path, more than double. Both start from the same impressive recent growth. Only one reflects what usually happens.
Link 2: Operating Margins
Margins tell you how much of each rupee of revenue survives competition and costs. Before forecasting a margin, ask three questions.
Where is the business in its cycle?
A cement or steel company's margin in a strong pricing year is not its normal margin. Use the average across a full cycle, often seven to ten years.
What does it depend on?
Paint makers depend on crude-linked raw materials, cement makers on coal, pet coke and diesel, and IT services firms on wage inflation and the rupee-dollar rate. If one of these moves, margins move.
Why would it expand?

Operating leverage, a better product mix or genuine pricing power can lift margins. "Management expects margin expansion" is not a reason. In a competitive industry, high margins attract new capacity, which pulls them back.

body.text: The most expensive forecasting mistake with cyclicals is extrapolating a peak year. When realisations spike, a company's EBIT margin can double. Carry that margin forward for ten years and your DCF will value the cycle's best moment as if it were permanent.

children.text: Link 3: Reinvestment That Matches Growth
Growth needs capital: new plants, new stores, more inventory, more receivables. A clean way to tie reinvestment to growth is the
sales-to-capital ratio

markDefs.definition: Revenue generated per rupee of invested capital. Dividing the increase in revenue by this ratio estimates how much net investment that growth requires.

body.caption: Reinvestment = capex net of depreciation + increase in working capital

children.text: Estimate the ratio from the company's own history, the change in revenue over five to ten years divided by the change in capital employed, and from peers. Capital-heavy businesses like cement, power and telecom have low ratios, often around 1. Asset-light businesses like IT services and branded consumer goods have much higher ratios, so each rupee of growth needs far less investment.

body.label: The consistency test
body.value: Return on new capital = Increase in NOPAT ÷ Cumulative reinvestment
body.context: If this implied return is far above anything the company or its industry has ever earned, your growth, margin or reinvestment assumptions do not agree with each other.

children.text: Worked Example: Two Forecasts for Kaveri Ridge Cement

Kaveri Ridge Cement sold 13 million tonnes last year at an average realisation of ₹5,000 per tonne, for revenue of ₹6,500 crore. EBIT was ₹1,000 crore, an EBIT margin of 15.4%. Installed capacity is 16 million tonnes a year, rising to 20 million tonnes once an expansion is commissioned over the next two years. Two analysts build five-year forecasts.
Analyst 1: the disciplined forecast
Revenue growth of 9% in year 1, from about 6.0% volume growth and 2.8% higher realisations, rising to 10% as new capacity comes on stream, then fading to 7% as it fills up.
EBIT margin held at 15.4%, its current level, with no assumed expansion.
Reinvestment tied to growth using a sales-to-capital ratio of 1.2, in line with the company's history and listed cement peers.
Analyst 2: the optimistic forecast
Revenue growth of 20% every year, extrapolating the company's best recent year.
EBIT margin rising steadily to 20% by year 5, because "operating leverage will kick in".
Reinvestment kept at last year's ₹200 crore, because "the big capex is behind us".

Each of the optimist's assumptions sounds defensible on its own in an earnings call. Put together, they claim Kaveri Ridge will earn about 168% after tax on every new rupee it invests, in an industry where after-tax returns in the low-to-mid teens are considered good. Revenue would reach ₹16,174 crore, roughly 2.5 times today's, while investing almost nothing. Even if realisations rose 3% a year, that revenue would require selling about 27.9 million tonnes of cement, far beyond the 20 million tonnes the plants can produce after the expansion. The disciplined forecast needs about 17.1 million tonnes on the same price assumption, around 85% utilisation. The disciplined forecast implies 13.8%, a little above the 11.5% WACC from the last lesson, which is what a well-run cement company can plausibly deliver.

body.text: Run the return-on-new-capital test on every forecast you build, and on every broker model you read. It takes two minutes, and it catches more bad valuations than any amount of fine-tuning the discount rate.

children.text: Seven Ways Investors Fool Themselves

cells: Flat recent history, then a sudden acceleration in year 2 of the forecast
Require a specific, dated reason: a plant, a product, a contract
Last year's growth or margin carried forward for a decade
Revenue compounds while capex and working capital stay flat
Tie reinvestment to growth with a sales-to-capital ratio
Steady margin expansion in a competitive industry
Name the source: mix, pricing power, operating leverage, and check peers
Every player in the industry is forecast to gain market share
Add up peer forecasts; market shares must total 100%
Management's earnings call targets copied into the model
Compare management's past guidance with what was actually delivered
Revenue forecast without inflation, discounted at a nominal rate that includes it
Keep both in nominal rupee terms, consistent with the G-sec-based discount rate

columns.label: Useful from an earnings call
points: Capacity additions, timelines and capex budgets
Commentary on raw material costs and pricing actions

columns.label: Treat with caution
points: Revenue or margin "aspirations" three to five years out
Guidance that is revised every quarter
Targets that exceed any past achievement
Growth plans without a stated funding plan

children.text: One Forecast Is Never Enough

Even a disciplined forecast is one path out of many. Build at least three: a base case you think is most likely, a bear case where the key risk materialises, and a bull case where things go right. Change the drivers that genuinely matter for the business, such as cement realisations, utilisation and new capacity from competitors, not every line by a fixed percentage. Chapter 3 shows how to weight and present these scenarios alongside the DCF value.
Check Your Understanding

body.title: Reinvestment needed for growth
body.prompt: A branded jewellery retailer's revenue is expected to grow from ₹2,000 crore to ₹2,500 crore next year. Its sales-to-capital ratio is 2.0. How much net reinvestment does that growth require, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Reinvestment = increase in revenue ÷ sales-to-capital = (₹2,500 - ₹2,000) ÷ 2.0 = ₹250 crore. For a jewellery retailer, much of this goes into inventory for new stores, not just the stores themselves.

body.title: Implied return on new capital
body.prompt: Your five-year forecast has a company's NOPAT rising by ₹60 crore while it reinvests a cumulative ₹400 crore. What return on new capital does your forecast imply, in %?
body.explanation: Return on new capital = ₹60 ÷ ₹400 = 15.0%. Compare this with the company's historical ROCE after tax, its WACC and its peers. If it looks sensible, your forecast hangs together.

body.title: Spot the inconsistent forecast
body.question: Which of these five-year forecasts for a mid-sized Indian paint company is internally inconsistent?
options: 12% revenue growth, stable margins, reinvestment rising in line with revenue
8% revenue growth, slightly lower margins as crude-linked input costs rise, moderate reinvestment
25% revenue growth, margins expanding by 5 percentage points, and capex falling every year while new plants and dealer networks are needed
15% revenue growth for three years, fading to 10%, with reinvestment tied to a historical sales-to-capital ratio
body.explanation: Faster growth than the industry, sharply rising margins in a competitive market and falling capex cannot all be true at once. High growth needs plants, tinting machines and dealer inventory, and competitors respond to rising margins. The implied return on new capital would be implausibly high.

body.title: Where growth settles
body.textWithBlank: Over the long run, a large company's revenue growth tends to fade toward the growth rate of the ___.
body.explanation: A company cannot outgrow the economy forever, or it would eventually become larger than the economy itself. Growth fades as markets mature and competition responds.

body.title: The QSR chain forecast
body.scenario: Shreya, an analyst at a Mumbai family office, is reviewing a colleague's forecast for a listed quick-service restaurant chain with 450 outlets. Management said on its latest earnings call that it targets 1,000 outlets in five years. The colleague's model has: revenue growth of 25% a year for ten years; EBITDA margin rising from 14% to 22% by year 5; capex flat at last year's level; and same-store sales growth of 8% a year throughout. Over the past five years, the company's same-store growth has averaged 4%, and two well-funded competitors are expanding aggressively in the same cities.
body.prompt: List the problems with this forecast and how Shreya should rebuild it.
body.modelAnswer:
Problems:
1. Growth without investment. Going from 450 to 1,000 outlets means opening about 110 stores a year, each needing fit-out capex and deposits. Flat capex cannot fund this.
2. Ten years of 25% growth. Management's own target covers five years. Extending it to ten ignores fading growth and market saturation.
3. Same-store growth of 8% is double the five-year average of 4%, with no stated reason.
4. Margin expansion from 14% to 22% while two funded competitors expand in the same cities. Competition usually pressures margins, and new stores typically run at lower margins before they mature.
5. Anchoring on guidance without checking management's track record on past store-opening targets.
6. Leases. A QSR chain's outlets are mostly leased. Under Ind AS 116, rent sits partly below EBITDA, so EBITDA margins are flattered. Lease payments must be treated consistently.

Rebuild:
1. Forecast revenue as outlets × revenue per outlet, with a realistic opening pace based on past delivery, and same-store growth near its historical average.
2. Fade total growth after year 5 toward nominal GDP growth.
3. Link capex to the number of new outlets using capex per store from past disclosures, and include deposits and working capital.
4. Hold margins near current levels in the base case, with expansion only in a bull case.
5. Check the implied return on new capital against the company's history and peers.
6. Build bear, base and bull scenarios around store openings and same-store growth.

body.title: Before you trust any forecast
steps: Is revenue built from real drivers such as volume × price or stores × revenue per store?
Does growth fade toward nominal GDP growth over time?
Is the margin assumption based on a full-cycle average, with a named reason for any expansion?
Is reinvestment tied to growth through a sales-to-capital ratio or explicit capex plan?
Is the implied return on new capital plausible against history, peers and WACC?
Have you compared management guidance with its past delivery?
Have you built bear, base and bull cases on the drivers that matter most?

points: A forecast is one connected story: revenue, margins and reinvestment must agree with each other.
Build revenue from real drivers, and let high growth fade toward nominal GDP growth over time.
Forecast margins from full-cycle averages and name a specific reason for any expansion.
Tie reinvestment to growth using a sales-to-capital ratio. Growth without investment is almost always an error.
Test every forecast with the implied return on new capital. Implausible returns reveal inconsistent assumptions.
Use management guidance for specifics like capacity and store openings, but check it against past delivery.
